Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is a severe fungal disease that affects both the leaves and fruit of apple trees. It significantly reduces fruit quality and yield if left unmanaged. The disease thrives in cool, wet spring weather where foliage remains wet for extended periods.
symptoms: Olive-green to black spots on leaves
Scabby, dark lesions on fruit
Yellowing and premature dropping of infected leaves
Deformed or cracked fruit in severe cases
causes: Fungal pathogen overwintering in fallen leaves
Prolonged leaf wetness during early spring
Poor air circulation within the tree canopy
treatment: Apply protective fungicides during early bud break
Use urea spray on fallen leaves to speed up decomposition
Prune infected branches to improve airflow
prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple varieties
Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn
Prune trees annually to ensure good canopy airflow
Maintain proper spacing between trees
Apple___Apple_scab.recommended_action: Apply a recommended fungicide and clear all fallen leaves from the orchard floor.

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot is a common fungal disease that can infect leaves, fruit, and branches of apple trees. It causes distinctive frogeye leaf spots and can lead to fruit decay and branch cankers. Warm, humid weather heavily favors its development.
symptoms: Purple spots on leaves that develop brown centers (frogeye appearance)
Brown-to-black rot on fruit, often starting at the calyx end
Sunken, discolored cankers on branches and limbs
Shriveled, mummified fruit remaining on the tree
causes: Fungus surviving winter in dead bark, cankers, and mummified fruit
Spores spreading via splashing rain
Tree wounds from pruning or weather damage providing entry points
treatment: Prune out and destroy infected branches and cankers
Remove all mummified fruit from the tree and ground
Apply appropriate fungicides starting at petal fall
prevention: Remove dead wood and plant debris from the orchard
Avoid excessive pruning during wet weather
Maintain tree health to resist infections
Apple___Black_rot.recommended_action: Prune out diseased wood immediately and apply a protective fungicide schedule.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar apple rust is a unique fungal disease that requires two different host plants to complete its life cycle: apple trees and eastern red cedars. It causes vibrant spotting on apple leaves and can defoliate trees if severe. The disease spreads rapidly during wet spring days.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper surface of leaves
Small orange tubular projections on the underside of leaves
Similar yellow-orange lesions on fruit
Premature leaf drop in severe infections
causes: Fungal spores blowing from infected cedar trees to apple trees
Spring rains triggering spore release from cedar galls
Proximity of apple orchards to eastern red cedar trees
treatment: Apply protective fungicides specifically timed for rust during early spring
Remove visible rust galls from nearby cedar trees if possible
Pick off heavily infected leaves on young apple trees
prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties
Remove eastern red cedar trees within a 1-to-2 mile radius of the orchard
Apply preventive fungicide sprays starting at the pink bud stage
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.recommended_action: Begin a protective fungicide program immediately if cedars are nearby and weather is wet.

Apple___healthy.description: The apple tree shows no visible signs of fungal, bacterial, or viral infections. The foliage is intact, brightly colored, and photosynthesizing normally. Maintaining optimal environmental conditions will help sustain this healthy state.
symptoms: Vibrant green leaves with no spotting or discoloration
Sturdy, blemish-free branches and trunk
Normal fruit development without lesions or rot
No signs of premature leaf drop
causes: Excellent genetic resistance or well-adapted variety
Proper orchard management and sanitation
Favorable weather conditions lacking prolonged moisture
treatment: No chemical treatment required at this time
Continue regular monitoring and scouting routine
Maintain current irrigation and fertilization schedules
prevention: Perform annual dormant pruning to maintain canopy airflow
Keep the orchard floor clear of fallen debris and mummified fruit
Ensure proper watering practices, avoiding overhead irrigation
Monitor weekly for early signs of pests or disease
Apple___healthy.recommended_action: Continue regular orchard maintenance and monitor weekly for any changes.

Blueberry___healthy.description: This blueberry bush is in excellent condition, displaying no signs of pathogens or pest damage. Proper soil acidity and moisture management are critical to keeping blueberries healthy. Continue standard care practices to ensure a good harvest.
symptoms: Lush green foliage with no spotting
Healthy cane growth without cankers or dieback
Normal flower and fruit cluster development
No signs of chlorosis (yellowing) on leaves
causes: Optimal soil pH (4.5 to 5.5)
Good drainage and appropriate moisture levels
Effective preventative care and field sanitation
treatment: No active disease treatment necessary
Maintain current nutritional program
Continue mulching to retain soil moisture and acidity
prevention: Monitor soil pH annually and adjust with elemental sulfur if needed
Prune out older canes during dormancy to encourage new growth
Ensure adequate irrigation, especially during fruit sizing
Keep the planting area weed-free to reduce pest habitats
Blueberry___healthy.recommended_action: Maintain optimal soil pH and continue routine care and watering.

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew on cherries is a common fungal disease that covers leaves and new shoots in a white, powdery fungal growth. It can stunt the growth of young trees and degrade fruit quality. Unlike many fungi, it thrives in warm weather with high humidity but does not require rainfall.
symptoms: White, powdery fungal patches on young leaves and shoots
Upward curling or blistering of infected leaves
Stunted or distorted shoot growth
White fungal growth on the surface of developing fruit
causes: Pathogen overwintering in buds and fallen leaves
High relative humidity combined with warm daytime temperatures
Poor air circulation in the orchard
treatment: Apply sulfur-based or systemic fungicides early in the season
Prune out heavily infected terminal shoots
Ensure thorough spray coverage on both sides of the leaves
prevention: Prune the canopy to increase sunlight penetration and air movement
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which promotes highly susceptible new growth
Implement a preventative fungicide schedule starting at petal fall
Keep orchard weed-free to lower ambient humidity
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.recommended_action: Apply an appropriate fungicide immediately and prune tree interior for better airflow.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: Gray leaf spot is a major yield-limiting fungal disease in corn, primarily affecting the foliage. It starts as small lesions that expand into rectangular, gray-to-brown spots that run parallel to leaf veins. High humidity, overcast days, and warm temperatures drive explosive outbreaks.
symptoms: Small tan spots with faint halos on lower leaves initially
Lesions elongating into blocky, rectangular gray/brown spots
Lesions restricted by leaf veins, creating a striped appearance
Severe blighting and death of entire leaves in late stages
causes: Fungal spores surviving winter on unburied corn residue
Extended periods of high relative humidity and heavy dew
Warm temperatures combined with overcast conditions
treatment: Apply foliar fungicides specifically rated for gray leaf spot
Time fungicide applications around the tasseling stage for maximum protection
Harvest heavily infected fields early to minimize stalk rot and lodging
prevention: Plant corn hybrids with high resistance ratings to gray leaf spot
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops like soybeans for 1-2 years
Use deep tillage to bury infected crop residue where appropriate
Manage weed populations to improve airflow in the lower canopy
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.recommended_action: Assess disease spread; if nearing the ear leaf before tasseling, apply a fungicide immediately.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern corn leaf blight is a fungal disease that causes large, cigar-shaped grayish-green lesions on corn leaves. If the disease establishes before tasseling, it can cause severe defoliation and significant yield loss. It thrives in moderate temperatures with heavy dew or frequent rain.
symptoms: Large (1-6 inch), long, elliptical or cigar-shaped lesions on leaves
Lesions initially grayish-green, turning tan or brown
Dark, fuzzy fungal sporulation appearing inside lesions during humid weather
Lesions merging to kill large sections of the leaf
causes: Fungus overwintering on infected corn debris in the field
Moderate temperatures combined with long periods of leaf wetness
Wind and splashing rain spreading spores to upper canopy
treatment: Apply preventative foliar fungicides if lesions appear before or during tasseling
Monitor weather closely, as dry weather naturally halts the spread
Harvest early if severe canopy loss threatens stalk integrity
prevention: Select corn hybrids with strong resistance packages
Rotate crops away from corn for at least one year
Incorporate infected crop residue into the soil via tillage
Manage weeds to ensure good airflow through the crop canopy
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.recommended_action: If lesions are reaching the ear leaf prior to tasseling, schedule a fungicide application.

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: This corn plant is healthy, showing vigorous growth and vibrant green foliage without any lesions, rust pustules, or blights. A strong, healthy canopy is essential for maximizing grain fill and overall yield. Continue standard agronomic practices.
symptoms: Deep green, uniform coloration across all leaves
No spots, streaks, or necrotic tissue on the foliage
Strong, upright stalks without signs of rot
Normal ear development and silk emergence
causes: Use of disease-resistant hybrids
Excellent soil fertility and nutrient management
Effective weed control and field sanitation
treatment: No fungicidal or chemical disease treatments required
Maintain current irrigation practices
Continue standard scouting procedures
prevention: Maintain appropriate crop rotation schedules
Ensure balanced fertilization, particularly nitrogen and potassium
Scout weekly for pests such as corn borers or earworms
Keep the field edges free of excessive weeds
Corn_(maize)___healthy.recommended_action: Maintain optimal irrigation and nutrient management to support grain fill.

Grape___Black_rot.description: Black rot is a highly destructive fungal disease of grapes that can completely wipe out a crop if unmanaged. It attacks all new growth, including leaves, shoots, and most critically, developing berries. The disease requires warm, wet conditions to release spores and infect tissues.
symptoms: Small, circular, reddish-brown spots on upper leaf surfaces
Black margins forming around leaf spots
Developing grapes turn light brown, then shrivel into hard, black, raisin-like mummies
Tiny black fruiting bodies (pycnidia) visible in leaf spots and on rotted fruit
causes: Fungus surviving winter in mummified berries and cane lesions
Spring rains causing spore release onto tender new growth
Extended periods of leaf and fruit wetness in warm weather
treatment: Apply effective fungicides starting from early shoot growth through berry touch
Prune out and destroy infected canes and clusters during the growing season
Remove all mummified fruit from the trellis and ground
prevention: Ensure excellent canopy management (leaf pulling) to increase airflow and sunlight
Remove and destroy all mummies during winter pruning
Maintain a strict preventative fungicide schedule during critical wet spring periods
Plant less susceptible grape varieties where possible
Grape___Black_rot.recommended_action: Apply a curative/preventative fungicide immediately and remove any visible mummified clusters.

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: Esca, also known as Black Measles, is a complex fungal trunk disease that slowly decays the wood of the grapevine from the inside out. Symptoms often suddenly appear on leaves and fruit during hot summer days. Because it resides inside the wood, it is notoriously difficult to treat once established.
symptoms: Tiger-stripe pattern on leaves (interveinal yellowing and browning)
Small, dark, purplish-black spots on white grape berries (measles)
Sudden wilting or collapse of parts or all of the vine (apoplexy)
White, spongy rot visible in the cross-section of the trunk or cordons
causes: A complex of fungal pathogens infecting pruning wounds
Pathogens colonizing and destroying the vine's vascular system
Hot, dry weather stressing the vine and exacerbating symptom display
treatment: Trunk renewal (cutting the trunk back to healthy wood and retraining a new shoot)
Remove and burn dead or dying vines to prevent spore spread
No foliar fungicides are effective against this internal wood disease
prevention: Delay winter pruning as late as possible to promote rapid wound healing
Apply wound protectants (fungicide pastes or biologicals) immediately after large pruning cuts
Double prune (rough prune early, make final cuts close to bud break)
Avoid making large pruning cuts on old wood during wet weather
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).recommended_action: Mark infected vines for trunk renewal or removal during the dormant season.

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: Grape leaf blight, also known as Isariopsis leaf spot, is a minor fungal disease that primarily affects the foliage late in the growing season. While it can cause premature defoliation, it generally does not cause significant economic loss unless the infection is exceptionally severe.
symptoms: Dark red to brown irregular spots on the leaves
Lesions enlarging and turning dark brown with dark borders
Drying out and crumbling of severely infected leaves
Premature dropping of affected foliage
causes: Fungus overwintering in fallen grape leaves on the vineyard floor
Warm, wet weather favoring spore germination
High humidity promoting fungal spread in dense canopies
treatment: Standard fungicide programs used for other grape diseases usually control this blight
Improve canopy aeration by shoot thinning and leaf removal
Remove heavily blighted leaves if the problem is localized
prevention: Shred and incorporate fallen leaves into the soil after harvest
Practice good canopy management to reduce humidity around the leaves
Maintain a baseline preventative fungicide program during the summer
Ensure proper vine nutrition to maintain plant vigor
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.recommended_action: Ensure the vineyard canopy has good airflow; specific chemical treatment is rarely needed.

Grape___healthy.description: This grapevine is showing excellent health with lush, green foliage and no signs of fungal spotting, trunk disease, or viral infections. Maintaining an open canopy and good soil drainage will keep the vine productive and resistant to disease.
symptoms: Uniform green leaves without spotting or yellowing
Healthy, vigorously growing shoots and tendrils
Clean, developing grape clusters without rot
Intact trunk and cordons with no oozing or cankers
causes: Excellent canopy management and airflow
Adherence to a preventative disease management schedule
Proper irrigation and nutritional balance
treatment: No therapeutic treatment required
Continue preventative care routine
Maintain standard vineyard monitoring
prevention: Conduct routine leaf pulling and shoot thinning to promote airflow
Keep the vineyard floor well-managed to reduce humidity
Continue preventative sprays for mildews and rots during high-risk weather
Ensure pruning tools are sanitized between vine blocks
Grape___healthy.recommended_action: Continue routine canopy management and monitor weekly for pests and diseases.

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: Citrus greening, or Huanglongbing (HLB), is the most devastating citrus disease worldwide. It is a bacterial infection spread by the Asian citrus psyllid that severely damages the tree's vascular system. Infected trees inevitably decline, produce bitter, misshapen fruit, and eventually die.
symptoms: Asymmetrical, blotchy yellow mottling on leaves
Thickened, leathery leaves with enlarged, corky veins
Small, lopsided, asymmetrical fruit that remain green at the bottom
Severe fruit drop, twig dieback, and overall tree decline
causes: Bacterium (Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus) blocking nutrient flow
Transmission by infected Asian citrus psyllids feeding on new flush
Propagation or movement of infected nursery stock
treatment: There is no cure for citrus greening
Aggressive nutritional support (foliar feeding) can temporarily prolong the productive life of infected trees
Severely declining trees must be removed and destroyed to protect nearby healthy trees
prevention: Implement aggressive chemical or biological control of the Asian citrus psyllid vector
Plant only certified, disease-free nursery stock from protected greenhouses
Scout orchards constantly and remove newly infected trees immediately
Use protective screening for young trees where practical
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).recommended_action: Immediately contact local agricultural authorities; the tree will likely need to be destroyed.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot is a damaging disease of peaches that affects leaves, twigs, and fruit. It often leads to severe defoliation, which weakens the tree and reduces the size and quality of the fruit. The bacteria are easily spread by wind-driven rain during warm weather.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked, angular spots on leaves that turn deep purple to black
Centers of leaf spots drop out, leaving a 'shot-hole' appearance
Deep, pitted, dark lesions on the skin of the fruit
Yellowing and severe dropping of infected leaves
causes: Bacteria overwintering in twig cankers and buds
Splashing rain and high winds spreading bacteria to new growth
Warm temperatures combined with high surface moisture
treatment: Apply copper-based bactericides during early spring/bud break
Apply oxytetracycline or other labeled bactericides during the growing season if pressure is high
Maintain optimal tree nutrition to help trees withstand defoliation stress
prevention: Plant peach varieties that are highly resistant to bacterial spot
Prune out visible twig cankers during the dormant season
Plant windbreaks around the orchard to reduce wind-driven rain spread
Ensure good airflow through the canopy via proper pruning
Peach___Bacterial_spot.recommended_action: Apply a labeled copper or antibiotic spray, and ensure proper orchard airflow.

Peach___healthy.description: This peach tree exhibits vigorous health, with unblemished foliage and no signs of bacterial spot or fungal rots. Proper pruning and proactive pest management are key to maintaining a productive and healthy peach orchard.
symptoms: Smooth, healthy green leaves without shot-holes or yellowing
Clean fruit development without pitting or fuzz discoloration
Sturdy branches without cankers or gummosis (oozing sap)
Vigorous new shoot growth
causes: Good orchard sanitation and disease resistance
Effective winter pruning and dormant spray applications
Optimal watering and nutritional support
treatment: No chemical intervention required
Maintain current cultivation practices
Monitor for insects like plum curculio and oriental fruit moth
prevention: Apply dormant copper or oil sprays annually to prevent overwintering diseases
Prune canopy in an open-center system to maximize sunlight and airflow
Thin fruit early in the season to prevent branch breakage and improve fruit size
Remove all dropped fruit from the orchard floor promptly
Peach___healthy.recommended_action: Maintain an open canopy via pruning and continue standard pest monitoring.

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot is one of the most destructive diseases of bell peppers. It causes severe spotting on leaves and fruit, leading to rapid defoliation and rendering the fruit unmarketable. The disease is explosive in hot, wet weather.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked, yellowish spots on leaves turning brown to black
Spots on fruit appearing as raised, blister-like scabs
Yellowing of the entire leaf followed by severe leaf drop
Sunscald on fruit due to sudden loss of the leaf canopy
causes: Seedborne or transplant-borne bacterial infection
Bacteria surviving on crop debris in the soil
Overhead irrigation or heavy rain splashing bacteria onto foliage
Hot, humid weather accelerating bacterial reproduction
treatment: Apply copper-based bactericides combined with mancozeb for better efficacy
Remove and destroy severely infected plants to prevent spread
Avoid working in the field when plants are wet
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds or hot-water treated seeds
Plant resistant bell pepper varieties
Rotate out of nightshade crops (peppers, tomatoes) for at least 2-3 years
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead watering to keep foliage dry
Deep plow crop residues immediately after harvest
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.recommended_action: Apply a copper-based bactericide immediately and switch to drip irrigation.

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: These bell pepper plants are healthy, showing no signs of bacterial spotting or viral distortion. A strong canopy of leaves is vital for shading the developing peppers and preventing sunscald. Keep plants well-watered and fed.
symptoms: Broad, dark green leaves with no spotting or yellowing
Strong, upright stems capable of supporting fruit weight
Smooth, firm, and unblemished developing peppers
Healthy flower production and fruit set
causes: Use of disease-free seed and resistant varieties
Optimal soil fertility and proper irrigation
Excellent field sanitation and crop rotation
treatment: No disease treatment needed
Continue regular watering
Maintain current fertilizer program
prevention: Water at the base using drip tape to avoid wetting the leaves
Maintain proper plant spacing for adequate airflow
Monitor regularly for aphids and thrips to prevent viral transmission
Stake or cage heavy plants to keep fruit off the soil
Pepper,_bell___healthy.recommended_action: Continue baseline care, prioritizing drip irrigation to keep foliage dry.

Potato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is a common fungal disease of potatoes that primarily targets older foliage. It reduces the photosynthetic area of the plant, which can result in smaller tubers and lower yields. It thrives in warm weather with alternating wet and dry periods.
symptoms: Small, dark brown spots on older, lower leaves
Spots enlarging to form concentric rings (target-board appearance)
Yellowing of tissue surrounding the spots
Dark, sunken, corky lesions on the tubers
causes: Fungus surviving in soil and infected plant debris
High humidity and heavy dew promoting spore germination
Nutritional stress, particularly low nitrogen, increasing susceptibility
treatment: Apply preventative or curative foliar fungicides
Ensure plants are receiving adequate nutrition, especially nitrogen
Harvest only fully mature potatoes to reduce tuber infection risk
prevention: Practice a 3-4 year crop rotation away from solanaceous crops
Plant certified disease-free seed potatoes
Ensure adequate fertilization and irrigation to prevent plant stress
Destroy potato cull piles and volunteer potatoes
Potato___Early_blight.recommended_action: Apply a targeted fungicide and check soil fertility, as stressed plants are more susceptible.

Potato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is a devastating water mold disease responsible for the Irish Potato Famine. It can rapidly destroy entire fields of potatoes in a matter of days under cool, wet conditions. The pathogen rots both the foliage and the tubers beneath the soil.
symptoms: Irregular, water-soaked, pale green to brown spots on leaves
White, fuzzy mold appearing on the undersides of leaves in humid conditions
Dark brown to black lesions on stems
Tubers developing shallow, reddish-brown, dry granular rot beneath the skin
causes: Oomycete pathogen surviving in infected seed potatoes and cull piles
Cool, wet, and highly humid weather driving rapid spore production
Spores washing down into the soil to infect tubers
treatment: Apply specific late blight fungicides immediately upon detection
Destroy heavily infected patches of the field via desiccation or burning to stop spread
Kill vines completely before harvest to prevent spores from contacting tubers
prevention: Plant certified, disease-free seed potatoes
Destroy cull piles and aggressively eliminate volunteer potato plants
Apply preventative fungicides when weather favors disease development
Hill up soil adequately around the base to protect tubers from spores
Potato___Late_blight.recommended_action: Apply an aggressive late blight-specific fungicide immediately; destroy heavily diseased patches.

Potato___healthy.description: These potato plants are vibrant and healthy, exhibiting no signs of foliar blights or viral infections. A robust canopy ensures maximum energy production for bulking up tubers underground. Continue best management practices.
symptoms: Full, deep green canopy of leaves
No target spots, white mold, or yellowing on foliage
Sturdy stems without dark lesions
Vigorous overall growth
causes: Use of high-quality, certified seed potatoes
Good field rotation and sanitation
Optimal soil moisture and nutrition
treatment: No chemical treatments needed for disease
Maintain current irrigation levels
Continue fertilization schedule as planned
prevention: Ensure proper hilling of soil to protect growing tubers from sun and spores
Scout regularly for Colorado potato beetles and aphids
Water deeply but infrequently, avoiding late-evening overhead irrigation
Maintain proactive preventative sprays if regional blight warnings are active
Potato___healthy.recommended_action: Maintain soil hilling and continue regular scouting for pests.

Raspberry___healthy.description: This raspberry plant is growing well, showing healthy canes and vibrant green foliage. Keeping the planting area weeded and properly pruned is vital to avoiding the fungal cane diseases that commonly affect raspberries.
symptoms: Bright green leaves without spotting, rust, or yellowing
Sturdy, healthy canes without purplish spots or cankers
Normal flower and fruit development
Vigorous emergence of new primocanes
causes: Good air circulation through proper pruning
Planting in well-drained soil
Excellent sanitation and disease resistance
treatment: No disease treatment is necessary
Maintain regular watering
Continue standard care
prevention: Prune out and destroy old fruiting canes immediately after harvest
Thin new canes to allow adequate sunlight and airflow
Maintain a narrow row width to improve canopy drying
Ensure good soil drainage, planting on raised beds if necessary
Raspberry___healthy.recommended_action: Continue proper pruning practices to ensure good airflow through the canes.

Soybean___healthy.description: The soybean crop is healthy, showing no signs of foliar diseases like rust or frogeye leaf spot. A complete, unblemished canopy is crucial for pod fill and maximizing yield. Maintain good agronomic practices to sustain crop health.
symptoms: Uniform green leaves without spotting or chlorosis
Strong stems and healthy trifoliate emergence
Normal flowering and pod development
No signs of wilting or stunted growth
causes: Planting of disease-resistant varieties
Proper crop rotation practices
Favorable weather conditions without excessive moisture
treatment: No disease interventions needed
Continue standard field management
Maintain routine scouting
prevention: Maintain strict crop rotation, alternating with non-legumes like corn
Ensure adequate row spacing to promote canopy airflow
Scout regularly for pests like aphids and stink bugs
Ensure adequate soil drainage to prevent root rots
Soybean___healthy.recommended_action: Continue standard field management and scout weekly for insect pests.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew is a highly prevalent fungal disease on squash and other cucurbits. It covers the foliage in a white, talcum-like powder, blocking photosynthesis. This causes early vine death, sunscald on fruit, and reduced yield.
symptoms: White, powdery fungal spots on the upper and lower leaf surfaces
Spots expanding to cover entire leaves, stems, and petioles
Leaves yellowing, turning brown, and shriveling
Premature vine decline and poor fruit flavor/size
causes: Windblown spores from warmer climates or nearby infected fields
High humidity promoting spore germination
Dense, shaded plant canopies reducing airflow
Dry leaf surfaces (rain actually inhibits this specific fungus)
treatment: Apply labeled fungicides, alternating modes of action to prevent resistance
Use organic options like sulfur, potassium bicarbonate, or neem oil early in infection
Remove and destroy severely affected leaves if the infection is localized
prevention: Plant powdery mildew-resistant squash varieties
Space plants widely to maximize sunlight and airflow
Control weeds to reduce humidity in the microclimate
Avoid excessive nitrogen applications which promote lush, susceptible growth
Squash___Powdery_mildew.recommended_action: Begin alternating fungicide applications immediately to protect remaining healthy foliage.

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: Leaf scorch is a common fungal disease of strawberries that causes the foliage to look burned or dried out. While it rarely kills the plant outright, severe infections reduce plant vigor, winter hardiness, and the following year's yield.
symptoms: Irregular purplish-brown spots on leaves without distinct centers
Spots coalescing to cover large areas of the leaf
Leaves curling upward and appearing burned or 'scorched' at the edges
Similar dark lesions on petioles and fruit runners
causes: Fungus overwintering on infected dead leaves and debris
Splashing rain or overhead irrigation spreading spores
Prolonged periods of leaf wetness during warm weather
treatment: Apply protective fungicides, especially during periods of frequent rain
Remove and destroy severely infected leaves if practical
Renovate strawberry beds aggressively after harvest
prevention: Plant resistant strawberry cultivars
Use drip irrigation to keep the foliage dry
Ensure proper spacing and weed control to promote rapid drying of leaves
Remove crop debris and old leaves during fall/winter
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.recommended_action: Apply a fungicide if rain is frequent, and switch to drip irrigation to keep leaves dry.

Strawberry___healthy.description: These strawberry plants are exceptionally healthy, displaying robust green leaves without signs of scorching, spotting, or mildew. Keeping the foliage dry and maintaining good spacing will keep them highly productive.
symptoms: Lush, green trifoliate leaves without dark spots or burned edges
Strong runners and petioles
Healthy, bright white flowers and firm red fruit
Vigorous crown growth
causes: Excellent cultural practices and sanitation
Adequate spacing and use of drip irrigation
Planting of disease-free crowns
treatment: No disease interventions needed
Maintain current watering regime
Continue standard fertilization
prevention: Water deeply using drip lines rather than overhead sprinklers
Use straw mulch to keep fruit off the soil and reduce splashing
Renovate beds immediately after the harvest season concludes
Ensure adequate spacing by managing runner density
Strawberry___healthy.recommended_action: Continue standard care, ensuring mulch is used to keep fruit off the bare soil.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot is a highly destructive disease in tomatoes, notorious for thriving in warm, wet weather. It aggressively attacks foliage and fruit, causing defoliation that leaves the remaining tomatoes highly susceptible to sunscald. The disease spreads rapidly via splashing rain.
symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves that rarely exceed 1/8 inch
Spots surrounded by yellow halos that eventually turn the whole leaf yellow
Raised, scab-like, dark lesions on the surface of green fruit
Significant dropping of lower leaves
causes: Infected seed or transplants bringing the bacteria into the field
Bacteria surviving on tomato debris and volunteer plants
Splashing rain, overhead watering, and high winds spreading the bacteria
Warm temperatures and high humidity driving bacterial reproduction
treatment: Apply copper-based bactericides combined with mancozeb for maximum efficacy
Avoid handling or working among the plants when foliage is wet
Remove heavily infected plants to slow the spread to healthy neighbors
prevention: Start with certified disease-free seed and transplants
Rotate crops, avoiding tomatoes and peppers in the same spot for 3 years
Use drip irrigation exclusively to keep foliage completely dry
Mulch heavily around the base of plants to prevent soil splashing
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.recommended_action: Apply a copper fungicide immediately, avoid overhead watering, and do not touch wet plants.

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is one of the most common fungal diseases of tomatoes, almost guaranteed to appear by mid-season. It usually starts on the lowest, oldest leaves and works its way up the plant. While it rarely kills the plant outright, it reduces yield and exposes fruit to sunscald.
symptoms: Brown-to-black spots on older, lower leaves
Spots enlarging into concentric rings resembling a target board
Extensive yellowing of tissue surrounding the spots
Dark, sunken, leathery lesions on the stem end of the fruit
causes: Fungus overwintering in soil and infected plant debris
Splashing rain or overhead irrigation lifting spores from soil to lower leaves
Warm temperatures and heavy dew or humidity
treatment: Prune off and discard severely infected lower leaves
Apply preventative or curative foliar fungicides
Ensure plants are well-fed; stressed plants succumb much faster
prevention: Provide excellent air circulation through staking or trellising
Mulch heavily beneath plants to act as a barrier against soil-borne spores
Water at the base of the plant only
Rotate planting locations away from nightshades annually
Tomato___Early_blight.recommended_action: Prune off the lowest infected leaves, apply mulch, and begin a fungicide program.

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is a catastrophic, highly contagious water mold that can completely destroy a tomato crop within a week. It requires cool, wet weather and spreads rapidly across entire regions via windblown spores. Infected plants appear as if they have been damaged by frost.
symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked, greasy-looking spots on leaves
White, fuzzy mold appearing on the underside of spots during high humidity
Dark brown to black lesions forming quickly on stems
Hard, brown, leathery rot spreading rapidly across the fruit
causes: Spores blowing in on weather systems from warmer regions
Cool, highly humid, and rainy weather
Proximity to infected potato crops or cull piles
treatment: Immediate application of specific late blight fungicides at first sign of disease
Bag and completely destroy (do not compost) infected plants to protect community crops
Harvest any mature green tomatoes immediately before rot sets in
prevention: Monitor local agricultural extension alerts for late blight in your area
Apply preventative fungicides preemptively when cool, wet weather is forecast
Ensure excellent airflow and rapid leaf drying through aggressive pruning
Destroy all volunteer tomatoes and potatoes near the growing area
Tomato___Late_blight.recommended_action: Bag and destroy infected plants immediately; apply late blight fungicides to any remaining healthy plants.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Tomato leaf mold is a fungal disease primarily found in high tunnels, greenhouses, or extremely humid climates. It causes distinctive fuzzy mold on the underside of leaves and leads to severe defoliation. The fungus thrives in stagnant, highly humid air.
symptoms: Pale green or yellowish spots on the upper surface of older leaves
Olive-green to brown, velvety fungal growth on the underside of the leaf spots
Leaves curling, withering, and dropping prematurely
Rarely affects the fruit directly, but defoliation stunts fruit growth
causes: Fungus surviving on crop debris and greenhouse structures
Prolonged periods of relative humidity above 85%
Poor air circulation within the greenhouse or dense crop canopy
Warm to moderate temperatures
treatment: Drastically improve ventilation and air movement
Apply approved fungicides early in the disease cycle
Prune off heavily infected lower foliage to reduce spore load
prevention: Ventilate greenhouses aggressively to keep humidity below 80%
Use fans to ensure constant air movement around the foliage
Prune plants to single or double leaders to reduce canopy density
Plant resistant tomato varieties, especially for indoor production
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.recommended_action: Immediately increase airflow/ventilation and prune off the worst infected lower leaves.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot is a rapidly spreading fungal disease that targets tomato foliage, usually starting after the first fruit sets. Unlike early blight, it causes numerous small spots and can defoliate a plant much faster, leaving fruit heavily exposed to sunscald.
symptoms: Numerous small, circular spots (1/16 to 1/8 inch) on lower leaves
Spots have dark brown margins with tan or gray centers
Tiny black specks (fruiting bodies) visible in the center of the spots
Rapid yellowing and dropping of infected leaves
causes: Fungus overwintering in soil and on weed hosts (like horsenettle)
Spores splashing onto lower leaves from rain or overhead watering
High humidity and moderate-to-warm temperatures
treatment: Apply foliar fungicides immediately upon spotting the first lesions
Remove and destroy severely spotted lower leaves
Avoid handling plants when they are wet to prevent spreading spores
prevention: Apply a thick layer of mulch to prevent soil from splashing onto leaves
Stake or cage tomatoes to keep foliage far off the ground
Water only at the base using drip irrigation
Practice a 3-year crop rotation away from solanaceous crops
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.recommended_action: Apply mulch to stop soil splashing, prune the lowest leaves, and apply a fungicide.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Spider mites are tiny arachnids, not a disease, but they cause severe damage to tomato plants by sucking sap from the leaves. They reproduce explosively in hot, dry, and dusty conditions. Heavy infestations cover the plant in fine webbing and cause the foliage to look bleached or sandblasted.
symptoms: Tiny yellow or white speckles (stippling) on the upper surface of leaves
Leaves taking on a faded, bronze, or silvery appearance
Fine, silk-like webbing visible on the undersides of leaves and at stem junctions
Premature leaf drop and severely stunted plant growth
causes: Hot, exceedingly dry weather
Dusty conditions, often near dirt roads or field edges
Overuse of broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural mite predators
treatment: Apply horticultural oils or insecticidal soaps, ensuring coverage on leaf undersides
Use specific miticides if populations are extremely high
Release predatory mites (like Phytoseiulus persimilis) in enclosed environments
prevention: Keep plants well-watered, as drought-stressed plants are highly susceptible
Spray foliage occasionally with a strong stream of water to wash off mites and disrupt webbing
Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides to preserve natural predators
Control weeds around the field edges where mites overwinter
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.recommended_action: Apply horticultural oil or insecticidal soap immediately, ensuring thorough coverage under the leaves.

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Target spot is a fungal disease that affects all parts of the tomato plant, causing lesions that resemble those of early blight. It is particularly damaging to the fruit, causing deep, rotting craters. The disease favors prolonged periods of high humidity and warm weather.
symptoms: Small, dark brown spots on leaves surrounded by pale yellow halos
Lesions enlarging to show concentric rings
Dark brown, sunken lesions on stems
Sunken, firm, dark rotting spots on the fruit that eventually crack open
causes: Fungus surviving on old crop debris and alternative weed hosts
Extended periods of leaf wetness and high relative humidity
Poor airflow through a dense plant canopy
treatment: Apply systemic or protectant fungicides at the first sign of disease
Remove and destroy heavily infected plants and fruit
Increase airflow by aggressively pruning the lower canopy
prevention: Ensure excellent crop rotation away from tomatoes and related weeds
Space plants generously and utilize trellising for maximum airflow
Avoid overhead watering and use mulch to prevent soil splashing
Apply preventative fungicides during periods of sustained high humidity
Tomato___Target_Spot.recommended_action: Prune out dense foliage to improve airflow and apply a broad-spectrum fungicide.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) is a devastating viral disease transmitted by the sweetpotato whitefly. It severely stunts the plant, halting new growth and fruit production. Once a plant is infected, it cannot be cured and must be removed to prevent further spread.
symptoms: Severe upward curling and cupping of the leaves
New leaves are noticeably reduced in size, thick, and crinkled
Yellowing (chlorosis) of the leaf margins and between veins
Extreme stunting of the plant and dramatic reduction in fruit set
causes: Transmission exclusively by the feeding of infected silverleaf/sweetpotato whiteflies
Infected transplants brought into the growing area
Proximity to other infected host plants or weeds
treatment: There is no cure or chemical treatment for virally infected plants
Immediately pull up and destroy (bag or burn) infected plants
Apply insecticides targeted at controlling the whitefly population
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant tomato varieties
Use reflective metallic mulches to repel whiteflies from young plants
Protect young transplants with fine mesh insect netting
Manage weeds in and around the field to eliminate whitefly resting sites
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.recommended_action: Remove and destroy the infected plant immediately; treat the area for whiteflies.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV) is a highly contagious viral disease that causes mottled, deformed foliage and stunted growth. It is primarily spread mechanically through contaminated hands, tools, or clothing, rather than by insects. While rarely fatal, it significantly reduces fruit quality and yield.
symptoms: Light and dark green mottled or mosaic pattern on leaves
Fern-like, stringy, or severely distorted leaf growth
Stunted overall plant vigor and reduced yields
Uneven ripening or internal browning of the fruit
causes: Transmission via contaminated hands, pruning tools, or clothing
Infected seeds passing the virus to transplants
Virus surviving in soil, root debris, and on greenhouse surfaces
treatment: There is no cure for mosaic viruses
Carefully remove and destroy infected plants immediately to prevent mechanical spread
Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water after handling infected plants
prevention: Plant virus-resistant tomato varieties (often denoted by 'T' in the seed catalog)
Disinfect pruning tools frequently with a bleach solution or commercial virucide
Avoid using tobacco products around plants (related viruses can be transferred)
Purchase certified disease-free seeds
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.recommended_action: Carefully remove and destroy the plant, then thoroughly wash hands and disinfect tools.

Tomato___healthy.description: This tomato plant is in excellent health, exhibiting vigorous growth, deep green foliage, and no signs of blights, wilts, or pest damage. Maintaining consistent soil moisture and good airflow are the keys to keeping it highly productive.
symptoms: Deep green, unblemished leaves without spots, curling, or yellowing
Strong, thick main stems capable of supporting heavy fruit
Abundant, healthy yellow blossoms
Smooth, firm developing fruit without rot or cracking
causes: Excellent preventative care and sanitation
Use of disease-resistant varieties and disease-free seeds
Optimal soil fertility, particularly calcium and phosphorus
treatment: No disease or pest treatments necessary
Continue regular, deep watering practices
Maintain current fertilizer schedule
prevention: Continue to prune bottom leaves to maintain a gap between soil and foliage
Water deeply and consistently to prevent blossom end rot and fruit splitting
Maintain a thick layer of mulch to conserve moisture and suppress weeds
Scout regularly for hornworms, aphids, and early signs of fungal spotting
Tomato___healthy.recommended_action: Maintain consistent deep watering and keep the lower canopy pruned for airflow.

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.description: The cherry tree is displaying normal, healthy growth without evidence of fungal, bacterial, or viral disease. The leaves are fully green and intact. Keeping the canopy well-pruned will help maintain this healthy status.
symptoms: Smooth, vibrant green leaves
No white powder, spots, or shot-holes on foliage
Healthy bark without oozing sap or cankers
Firm, developing fruit with no rot
causes: Favorable growing conditions and climate
Proactive disease management and pruning
Adequate soil drainage and nutrition
treatment: No disease interventions needed
Continue standard watering practices
Maintain regular orchard walk-throughs
prevention: Prune annually to maintain an open canopy for light and air
Avoid overhead irrigation to keep foliage dry
Harvest fruit promptly when ripe to avoid attracting pests
Monitor for aphids and fruit flies
Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.recommended_action: Continue regular monitoring and ensure the tree canopy has good airflow.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Common rust is a widespread fungal disease of corn characterized by powdery, brick-red pustules on the leaves. While highly visible, it usually occurs late enough in the season that it does not significantly impact yield on resistant commercial hybrids. It favors cool, humid conditions.
symptoms: Small, powdery, brick-red to brown pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces
Pustules elongated or oval-shaped, breaking through the leaf epidermis
Yellowing of leaf tissue surrounding the pustules
Pustules turning black as the corn plant matures
causes: Spores blown in by wind from southern climates
Cool temperatures combined with high humidity and heavy dews
Planting highly susceptible sweet corn varieties
treatment: Fungicides are rarely necessary for commercial field corn
In susceptible sweet corn, early fungicide application may be warranted if pressure is high
Monitor disease progression on the upper canopy
prevention: Plant modern, rust-resistant corn hybrids
Plant corn early in the season to avoid peak spore flights
Ensure proper field drainage to reduce micro-canopy humidity
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.recommended_action: Monitor the crop; treatment is usually only needed for highly susceptible sweet corn varieties.
